newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia to resume coca eradication next week.
newsitem.headline: Colombia to resume coca eradication next week.

text.p: Colombia, which shocked the United States by suspending the aerial spraying of its coca crops, will resume the eradication of the plant used to make cocaine, Justice Minister Carlos Medellin said on Friday.

He told a news conference the aerial spraying programme, which was suspended on Wednesday in apparent reprisal for Washington's decision to "decertify" Colombia for a second year as an ally in the drug war, would resume next week.

"Aerial coca eradication operations in Colombia will restart as of next Wednesday," Medellin said after a closed-door meeting of the national anti-drugs council. He said the operation had been suspended only temporarily while police and government officials reviewed its effectiveness in light of what U.S. officials have described as a 32 percent increase in the cultivation of coca last year.

That jump, which made Colombia the world's second largest grower of the raw material for cocaine, was cited among other reasons for Washington's decision last week to leave it on a blacklist of countries that have failed to cooperate fully with the United States in global anti-drug efforts.

The suspension of aerial spraying caught U.S. officials off guard and drew a rebuke from State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, who said Washington reserved the right to clamp economic sanctions on Colombia.

U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette, who urged a quick resumption of eradication operations by the world's largest producer of cocaine, had warned that the suspension could spell "disaster" for already difficult U.S.-Colombia ties.

Colombian officials have openly questioned the U.S. figures on coca production, arguing that they fail to take into account areas that had actually been sprayed as part of the U.S.-backed programme that has claimed the lives of 35 pilots and anti-drug fighters since 1995.

To ensure that no such disputes will occur in the future, Medellin said he and the head of the anti-narcotics division of the National Police would travel to Paris this month to ask the French government for assistance in monitoring Colombia's illicit drug crops with a so-called spy-in-the-sky satellite.

In a clear swipe at the United States, he said it was "very important" to obtain independent verification of U.S. crop estimates. He also said no decision had been made on U.S.-backed moves to replace the liquid herbicide currently in use in Colombia with a more effective granular variety.

U.S. contract pilots began working with Colombian police in the drug fumigation programme last year. One was killed in January when his crop-duster aircraft crashed in a guerrilla-controlled area in southeast Colombia.
Colombia's leading leftist guerrilla group, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, obtains much of its funds through protection of rural drug farms and laboratories.
Colombia also accounts for 1.5 percent of the world's opium production. Medellin said aerial spraying of opium poppy had not been halted when spraying of coca was this week.
